implementation_notes: A C# class owns its parts as fields; the garbage collector reclaims ordinary memory but never resource lifetime, so a whole that holds disposables implements IDisposable and cascades Dispose to the parts it owns - explicitly not to parts it merely borrowed - while callers scope that release with `using` statements or declarations. The framework guidelines concentrate the real cleanup in Dispose(bool) (false when called from the finalizer path), recommend SafeHandle instead of hand-written finalizers for unmanaged handles, and require Dispose to be idempotent. Ordinary composition plus the dispose pattern replaces the classic Whole/Part role split; an explicit whole class still earns its place for lazy or runtime-configurable parts, where the whole decides when a part comes into existence.
pitfalls: A finalizer runs on an unspecified thread at an unspecified time and must not touch other managed objects (they may already be finalized); keep cleanup in Dispose(bool) and let SafeHandle own unmanaged handles.
Dispose must be idempotent and must cascade only to owned parts; disposing a borrowed IDisposable surprises the caller who still uses it.
Lazy part creation inside a property getter races two threads into two parts; use Lazy<T> or locking, and remember that Lazy<T> itself releases nothing on Dispose.
